statements.text: A UK government spokesperson said Ukraine has repeatedly shown it is serious about peace, while Russia has repeatedly rejected full and partial ceasefires and continues attacks on Ukrainian civilians and energy, and that Russia could end the war today.

A UK government spokesperson said the UK will continue working with international partners to ensure Ukraine has the military and financial support it needs, will maintain pressure on Russia through the toughest sanctions regime ever imposed by the UK, remains committed to supporting Ukraine for as long as it takes, and fully supports US-led efforts to secure a just and lasting peace.

In a statement to the Commons, the Prime Minister said an energy ceasefire, with both sides stopping their attacks, is the quickest way to get diesel back onto world markets without rewarding the aggressor, and that Ukraine wants one. He welcomed President Trump's announcement of a reciprocal energy ceasefire, and said President Zelenskyy has assured him Ukraine would implement it immediately once a start date is confirmed.

In a statement to the Commons on 12 October, the Prime Minister said the UK has announced new funding to help Ukraine get through its fifth winter under Russian bombardment, and a new sanctions package covering over 90% of Russia's oil producing capacity.

The Prime Minister told the Commons that Russian strikes have intensified in the three weeks since his meeting with President Zelenskyy in New York, with attacks on apartment blocks and on buses carrying children. He said Zelenskyy had described a step change from Russia, including daylight attacks intended to break Russia's will and Ukraine's, and said that will never happen.

The Prime Minister told the Commons the UK assesses it is highly likely the incident at RAF Fairford was coordinated in Iran and almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard. He said the UK will not tolerate these threats, will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks, and will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do the UK harm.

The Prime Minister confirmed the UK-EU summit will take place in Brussels on 20 November. On the table, he said, are a trade deal on food and drink, a deal on emissions trading and progress towards linking energy systems, a new youth experience scheme, and deeper cooperation on immigration.

The Prime Minister said a food and drink trade deal would add the equivalent of over £10 billion a year to the UK economy by 2040, with potential for significantly more. The agreement on the table is expected to lift a burden of up to £1,400 on a single shipment for farmers and food producers, to end export health certificates costing up to £200 each time for small businesses, and to ease pressure on supermarket prices.

The Prime Minister said current border rules cost trade: truckloads of plants or produce can be destroyed over a missing stamp, fresh meat and fish spoil in trucks, Scottish salmon faces a 100% rate of document checks costing around £100 million in lost exports, British fresh meat cannot be sold in the EU, and seed potatoes from Scotland and shellfish from Wales are banned.

The Prime Minister said the agreement on the table could help lower energy costs for households and businesses, and that the proposed energy deal could cut wholesale energy costs in Northern Ireland by 20%.

On immigration, the Prime Minister said a deal could link up law enforcement efforts again, sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals, and faster electronic evidence from the phones of those behind gangs.

The Prime Minister said the UK will meet its NATO commitments in full. He said that in Berlin he and Chancellor Merz agreed a new partnership to tackle Russian hybrid threats, and confirmed a commitment to establish a new National Centre for Information Defence.

The Prime Minister confirmed Britain's decision to send air defence and a Voyager aircraft to Saudi Arabia for air-to-air refuelling, and said a Voyager has already completed 14 operational missions. He condemned the appalling attacks on King Khalid International Airport and said the UK will continue to stand with Saudi Arabia against the Houthis.

The Prime Minister said that since the UN General Assembly the UK has been in close contact with the US about protective security at shared bases, and thanked police and military personnel for their swift response to incidents at RAF Fairford and RAF Molesworth. The Home Secretary is to update the House on Fairford.

The Prime Minister said he raised with President Trump the Falkland Islands and the clear and declared will of the islanders to remain British, and said the UK will always do whatever it takes to uphold the islanders' will.

The Prime Minister said he believes the UK's chances of a summit deal will be enhanced by being open to discussing the relationship with the EU in the longer term. He said the immediate priority is the summit, after which a serious dialogue on options should follow, with the British public as the boss at every stage and public opinion currently supporting a pragmatic approach.

The Prime Minister said the UK will take up the G20 presidency in 2027 and place AI centre stage, capturing its opportunities while guarding against its risks, with the aim of agreeing a single set of global principles and standards on AI during its presidency year.

The Prime Minister has asked Ministers to draw up further sanctions, military aid and fiscal packages to provide urgent support in the coming weeks, and was set to tell President Zelenskyy so, including accelerating delivery of critical air defence missiles.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK's rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping the UK safe and for ensuring those on the frontlines have the equipment to push back Russia. He said the UK is with Ukraine for as long as it takes and will go further and faster, that this is not just the right thing but the necessary thing, and that Russia's aggression cannot be allowed to succeed on the continent.

The UK will accelerate deliveries of British Lightweight Multirole Missiles, which have proven extremely effective against jet-powered drones; these are faster and fly higher than Shaheds and are harder to detect and destroy. The UK has already committed £1.6 billion to deliver more than 5,000 such missiles over four years, and will accelerate £10 million of the £45 million package announced today to meet Ukraine's most urgent winter requirements.

speakers: Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey
statements.text: The UK is standing by plans to fully implement a maritime services ban on Russian LNG exports. Chancellor John Healey is urging partners at the IMF meetings in Bangkok to implement an equivalent ban, after the Foreign Secretary did the same at the Warsaw Security Forum. Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey said he urges partners to back the ban to curtail the war chest funding Putin.

The Prime Minister welcomed President Zelenskyy to Downing Street on 14 October. The leaders reflected on their call on Saturday and on Russia's blatant indiscriminate attacks on civilians and energy infrastructure since President Trump called for an energy ceasefire, and underlined that Russia had no interest in peace.

The Prime Minister set out the UK's latest package of Lightweight Multirole Missiles to help Ukraine's allies respond to Russia's jet-powered drones, and the leaders discussed how the UK could accelerate defensive support ahead of winter. The Prime Minister said the UK would continue developing innovative military solutions, including retrofitting British capability onto equipment gifted by other partners, and continue its diplomatic efforts to support international supplies of defensive equipment.

Great British Railways' headquarters is to be at Becketwell, a brownfield site in Derby city centre, which will accommodate up to 450 GBR staff. Construction is expected to begin in early 2027 and be completed by spring 2029. The HQ is estimated to bring hundreds of rail jobs and a £151 million boost to Derby's economy, a milestone in the government's plan for a publicly owned railway.

Up to 600 apprentices aged 16 to 21 will enrol over the next four years on the rail foundation apprenticeship, with the first starters based in Derby. The government says this matters because less than 7% of the railway's workforce is under 25.

Andy Burnham said people have put up with a railway that often lets them down, that today is another big step forward, and that Great British Railways' home in Derby will bring investment and good jobs, giving young people the chance to build their future there.

Heidi Alexander said the biggest shake-up to the railways in a generation is underway, with Great British Railways working around one mission of better services for passengers. She said she is delighted Becketwell will become GBR's new home, and that with 600 apprenticeships opening up the government is investing in the people who will build the railway.

Pat McFadden said the government is determined to build the strong pipeline of skilled workers a thriving rail sector depends on, and that the foundation apprenticeship lets young people explore career paths while earning. He said it forms part of a £2.5 billion youth employment support package creating up to 500,000 opportunities to earn or learn.

Claire Ward called it fantastic news for Derby, said that Great British Railways being based there brings hundreds of jobs, and said she is particularly pleased about the 600 apprenticeship places, so young people can build a career without having to move away.

The Prime Minister will invite the First Minister to work with him to push more power out of both Westminster and Holyrood. He will ask the Scottish Government to work with the UK government through No10 North and the Scotland Office to develop a new model of regional empowerment for Scotland.

Andy Burnham said that in his first week in office he told the First Minister he wanted to work with him to spread opportunities across Scotland's regions, that through No10 North the government is rewiring the state and he wants Scottish regions fully part of it, and that this is him making an offer to the Scottish Government.

Douglas Alexander said devolution has done a great deal but power was never supposed to stop at the doors of the Scottish Parliament, and that people in North Lanarkshire, Fife or the Highlands know their needs better than any minister. He called the Prime Minister's offer to the Scottish Government a genuine one, and said the Scotland Office is ready to help make it happen.

In his speech in Motherwell on 16 October, the Prime Minister said he was making a serious and genuine offer to the Scottish Government. He said he wants to design together, in the months ahead, a new model of regional economic empowerment across Scotland that puts control in the hands of local people, and that at UK level the government is looking at devolving innovation, enterprise and employability funding to match Scotland's strengths.
The Prime Minister offered Scotland DWP devolution, a model of localised employment support similar to England's but shaped by Holyrood and right for Scotland.

The Prime Minister said that in a couple of weeks the National Economic Council will meet the First Ministers of Scotland and Wales and the First Minister and Deputy First Minister of Northern Ireland, for the first time since he became Prime Minister, to put the offer on the table and see if a plan can be worked out together.

The Prime Minister said that in August 2023 he visited FARE-Scotland at Easterhouse, where he had expected to talk about policing, drugs and violence but talked only about empowerment and opportunity. He said he took what he learned back to Greater Manchester and used it to pioneer the Live Well model.
The Prime Minister said the review led by Alan Milburn is challenging the government to build a system based on the Easterhouse principle of names not numbers, built from the bottom up.
The Prime Minister said around one in six young people in Scotland are not in education, employment or training.

The Prime Minister said around one in twenty shops in Edinburgh is lying empty, against around one in five in Dundee, and that a man in East Renfrewshire can live on average seven years longer than a man in Glasgow, as he understood it.

The Prime Minister said devolution was never meant to stop at the doors of the Scottish Parliament, and that Scotland, the most devolved nation in the UK, has become one of the most centralised nations in Europe.

The Prime Minister said the government is already giving English local leaders more power and control over transport, more say over skills and investment, and more freedom to build an economy around their communities' strengths, and that he wants the same opportunities for Scotland and Scottish regions.
The Prime Minister said the Scottish government has this week agreed to match the UK government's £10 million to create two defence technical excellence colleges, one in the east and one in the west.

The Prime Minister said that as Mayor of Greater Manchester he put buses back under public control and chose buses built by Alexander Dennis in Falkirk, and that he wants all public procurement in the UK to back a plan to reindustrialise Britain.

The Prime Minister said the UK is putting a billion pounds into research and innovation in the coming years, and that English mayors already have more control over funding for local innovation. He wants to explore how Scotland's regions can have the same powers to decide where research and development investment goes.

The Prime Minister told John Swinney he wants to push economic power out into Scotland's regions, asked whether he does, and proposed agreeing a new process, working with Douglas Alexander and John Swinney's team, and a new proposal right for Scotland that the two governments work on together.
